U0.p: A general heading for stories about the unequal conditions of life, such as why some people have much and others little.

U10.p: A general heading for stories about justice and injustice.

U11.p: Petty wrongdoing is punished harshly while serious crimes by powerful people are overlooked.

U11.1.p: An ass is punished for stealing a mouthful of grass, while a lion and a wolf go unpunished for eating sheep.

U11.1.1.p: The animals confess their sins to one another; the fox and wolf forgive each other and the ass is punished.

U11.1.1.1.p: The animals confess their sins to a lion who sits as judge; all the powerful animals are forgiven while the ass and lamb are punished.

U11.1.1.2.r: *Wesselski Arlotto I 191 No. 17; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
U11.1.1.2.p: A penitent in confession worries about his little sins and makes light of the big ones.

U11.2.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 351; Scala Celi 20a No. 120; Alphabet No. 334; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
U11.2.p: The person who steals a lot is called a king, and the person who steals a little is called a robber.

U11.2.1.p: A wolf is punished for theft while kings are honored, despite their own thefts.

U12.p: The heaviest burdens are put on the smallest asses, and the best offices go to the most ignorant men.

U14.p: Unworthy people are rewarded while the deserving are passed over.

U15.r: (1) Sees a man who is to die that day buy shoes. (2) Sees sheriff leading a man to the gallows: a big thief leading a little one. (3) Sees farmer weeping at funeral of his child, while priest (the real father) sings. Wesselski Mönchslatein 193 No. 153.
U15.p: A fool laughs at the absurdities he sees around him.

U15.0.1.r: (1) Sees man who is to die that day complain that his shoes are too thin. (Cf. J2174.) (2) Sees women adorn their heads when they are immoral below. (Cf. J2050.) (3) Sees man remove from his wife’s garment dust gathered while she lay with another man. (Cf. J2301.3.) (4) Sees persons making plans while forgetting to say, “If God wills.” Irish myth: *Cross.
U15.0.1.p: A dwarf king, who is a fairy, laughs at the absurdities he sees around him.

U15.1.p: A philosopher laughs at the vanities and sins of the world, while his companion weeps.

U18.p: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and so the children's teeth are set on edge, meaning children suffer for their parents' faults.

U21.p: What counts as justice depends on one's point of view.

U21.1.p: A hen complains that man eats her, but she herself eats ants.

U21.2.p: A gift of property silences criticism, as when a priest who has preached against lucrative church posts falls silent after receiving one.

U21.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 77 (ET 429), 103 (ST 161); Halm No. 118; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 11, Beal XXI 305.
U21.3.p: A man complains that the gods unjustly wrecked a ship because of one man's sin, then kills a whole swarm of ants because one of them stung him.

U21.4.p: A wolf objects when a lion steals sheep from him, although he himself has stolen that sheep.

U21.5.p: A judge reduces the penalty when the accused is his own son.

U25.p: Theft committed to avoid starvation is forgiven.

U27.p: A swallow whose young is killed in a court of law by a snake complains that injustice is done in the house of justice. The courts fail to protect the weak.

U30.p: The idea that the powerful take what they want from the weak, since might makes right. This is a general heading for tales about inequality in life.

U31.r: U141.) Wienert FFC LVI 50 (ET 97), 148 (ST 526); Halm Aesop No. 274; *Crane Vitry 191 No. 135; Herbert III 12; Alphabet No. 631; Jacobs Aesop 199 No. 2; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 83 (monkey and goat).
U31.p: A wolf falsely accuses a lamb of wrongdoing, though the lamb answers every charge, and then eats him anyway, claiming his right as the stronger.

U31.1.p: A cat falsely accuses a cock, and even though the cock answers every charge well, the cat eats him, saying she can no longer go hungry.

U31.2.p: A crow asks a dove to sing so that the crow can use the song to kill her young; after the dove sings, the crow kills the brood anyway, using his strength over the helpless dove.

U32.r: Wienert FFC LVI 64 (ET 273), 146 (ST 513); Halm Aesop No. 209.
U32.p: A hunter insists on killing a lark even though she has taken only a single grain of wheat, so the smallness of her offense does not save her.

U33.p: A rooster who pleads that he is useful to people is killed by his captors anyway.

U34.p: A nobleman murders a common person and goes unpunished because of his rank.

U34.1.p: A nobleman who has killed a common person is finally brought to justice, but only after a long delay.

U35.r: Herbert III 40ff. No. 39; Hervieux IV No. 40; Irish myth: *Cross.
U35.p: A rich man, here a king, takes the cow of a poor widow or nun, abusing his power over someone without means.

U35.1.p: A king seizes an old woman's cow for himself.

U35.1.1.p: A king seizes a poor man's lamb for himself.

U35.2.p: Nobles ruin a peasant's or widow's crops and suffer no consequences.

U36.r: Wienert FFC LVI 50 (ET 92), 129 (ST 367); Halm Aesop No. 395.
U36.p: A bull kills a lion cub, and when the lioness complains, she has no right to do so because of what happened to her cub.

U37.r: Wienert FFC LVI 47 (ET 58), 103 (ST 157); Halm Aesop No. 281.
U37.p: A wolf, acting as commander, orders all the spoils of a raid divided fairly, but quietly keeps the largest share for himself.

U38.p: A ruler banishes a subject for a trivial or harmless remark.

U41.p: A ruler forces a bishop to ordain a priest who is ignorant and unfit for the office.

U42.p: Advice to flatter a master: approve of whatever he likes and condemn whatever he dislikes, whatever you really think.

U60.p: A general heading for tales about the contrast between wealth and poverty.

U61.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 233 No. 509, Bebel I 232 No. 149, Mensa Philosophica No. 63.
U61.p: God is said to divide things so that the poor receive little and the rich receive much, a bitter remark about unfair shares in the world.

U63.p: A priest who is ignored while poor suddenly gains many friends once he is made a bishop, showing that people value status more than the man himself.

U65.p: A beggar who owns a horse, a wife, or a dog is seen as rich by an even poorer beggar, showing that wealth depends on who is looking.

U65.1.p: Even the poorest person, who has only grass to lie on, finds it a comfortable bed, so comfort is measured against one's own poverty.

U66.p: Everyone can be bought if the price is right; no one is so honest that money cannot tempt them.

U66.1.p: The same saying applied to women: every woman can be won over for a price.

U66.1.1.r: Jester replies, “If a man have goods enough, he might have a sovereign lady.” England, U.S.: *Baughman.
U66.1.1.p: A man keeps raising his offer for a queen's favors, and she is ready to yield once he reaches a high enough sum, but she hesitates when the offer is raised again.

U67.p: A jester takes a cow from a poor peasant and tells the king that the people have plenty of milk, because a man who is warm thinks everyone else is warm too.

U68.p: A man who always looks on the bright side becomes gloomy and pessimistic once he has been robbed of his money.

U71.p: A man is so constantly blessed with wealth by God that he cannot manage to give away all his goods to the poor.

U81.p: Owning much property brings many dangers and worries, so wealth is a burden as well as a benefit.

U81.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 44 (ET 21), 141 (ST 470); Halm Aesop No. 358.
U81.1.p: A dove is proud of her large brood of young but is also anxious that she might lose them.

U83.p: A king who has been exiled is ignored by everyone, but when he regains his throne, people come to court him again.

U84.p: The same object has different prices depending on the place where it is sold.

U110.p: Things are not always what they seem; a person's outward appearance may hide the truth about them.

U111.p: Simply owning or carrying many books does not make someone learned or a scholar.

U111.1.p: A young person pretends to be a scholar by carrying a large stack of books to fool his mother, but the books do not make him learned.

U112.p: A beard on a she-goat does not make it a male; a surface feature does not change what a thing truly is.

U113.r: (Frogs, crickets.) Wienert FFC LVI 61, *66 (ET 232, 304), 123 (ST 321, 322); Halm Aesop Nos. 172, 248.
U113.p: A creature with a very loud voice turns out to be small and insignificant.

U114.r: Wienert FFC LVI *44 (ET 24), *101 (ST 141); Jacobs Aesop 203 No. 14; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
U114.p: A great fuss or threat ends in a tiny result, as when a mountain strains in labor and gives birth to only a mouse.

U115.r: An apparently happy man lets another see the actual misery of his existence. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 223.
U115.p: A family secret or shameful hidden fact that is kept out of sight behind a closed door.

U115.1.p: A woman who seems cheerful and content reveals that she has been keeping the skeleton of her murdered lover, showing that appearances can hide a grim secret.

U116.p: A hypocrite who pretended to be pious is honored as a saint after he dies, even though his true character was false.

U117.p: A man turns down a bride because she looks too young, but her father assures him she has already borne several children.

U119.p: A general heading for other tales in which things are not what they seem and outward appearance misleads.

U119.1.p: A satyr, a wild woodland creature, exposes hidden truths about people, revealing what is really going on behind respectable appearances.

U119.1.1.p: At a child's funeral a satyr reveals that the priest conducting the service is the real father, and that the grieving husband who thinks he is the father is the one who weeps while the priest sings.

U119.1.2.p: At a hanging, the onlookers turn out to be bigger thieves than the man being hanged, so the crowd is more guilty than the condemned culprit.

U119.2.p: A peasant envies the monks, thinking their life is very easy, and wishes to trade places with them, but after one night in the monastery he changes his mind.

U119.3.p: A handsome person is not necessarily good: an angel holds its nose when a handsome sinner walks by, showing that good looks do not reveal a beautiful soul.

U119.4.p: An ugly person can have a noble, holy soul: a very ugly man proves to be a saintly person despite his appearance.

U119.5.p: Stories showing that a person's name does not change what they really are or their social condition.

U120.p: A general heading for stories holding that a person's true nature or origin will eventually come out, whatever they pretend.

U121.p: Children inherit the traits of their parents, so their true nature shows as they grow up.

U121.1.r: *Crane Vitry 152 No. 44; Wienert FFC LVI *63 (ET 258), *103 (ST 159); Halm Aesop No. 187.
U121.1.p: A crab walks backward, having learned this from its parents, showing that young creatures copy their parents.

U121.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI *63 (ET 256), 103 (ST 158, 501); Halm Aesop No. 130.
U121.2.p: A young deer, like its mother, runs away from the hounds; it is useless for her to urge him to stand and fight.

U121.3.p: The son of a farmer and the son of a noble are raised in the country, yet the farmer's son takes to farm work while the noble's son takes to riding and hunting, showing that breeding shows.

U121.4.p: A man claimed to be a king's son is shown to be a bastard when he displays the habits of his real father.

U121.5.p: A father acts foolishly at the king's court, just as his son does, showing the foolishness runs in the family.

U121.6.p: The son of a butcher grows up to be a cruel and atrocious ruler, showing the trait passed down from his father.

U122.r: Wienert FFC LVI 60 (ET 217), 119 (ST 292); Halm Aesop No. 185; Herbert III 35ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
U122.p: A dung beetle prefers the smell of its dunghill to any other smell, showing that each creature likes what suits its own nature.

U122.1.p: Beetles given the same honor as oxen still will not act like oxen; a dung beetle keeps preferring its dunghill to any other smell. Nature cannot be changed by outside treatment.

U123.p: A hog is taken to a bath but goes back to wallowing in mud. Its true nature wins out over what it is given.

U124.p: A scorpion carried across a stream on a turtle's back stings it anyway, even though this drowns them both. It cannot help its sting.

U125.r: Chauvin II 125 No. 123; Scala Celi 50b No. 285; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
U125.p: A wolf listening to a sermon loses interest as soon as he sees a flock of sheep. His appetite beats his piety.

U125.1.p: A heron or crane loses interest in heaven if there are no snails to eat there. Its appetite outweighs any promise of paradise.

U126.p: A dog allowed to warm itself inside a house starts barking, and is chased back out. It cannot resist acting like a watchdog even when it is shown kindness.

U127.r: Wienert FFC LVI 63 (ET 257), 89 (ST 12): Halm Aesop No. 303.
U127.p: A fawn with fine horns still runs away from a dog. Its fear is stronger than its useful weapons.

U128.p: A tiger born to a human mother scratches her and licks her blood. Its wild nature shows despite its human upbringing.

U128.1.p: A tiger that is the father of a human child licks the child's blood. The animal nature of the tiger shows even in its human offspring.

U129.p: A general case in which a creature's or person's true nature reveals itself no matter how it is disguised or raised. This entry gathers the miscellaneous tales of this kind.

U129.1.p: A fox's natural thievishness shows itself, however it is treated. It keeps stealing.

U129.2.p: A prostitute deceives a new lover just as she has always deceived others. Her habit of deceit does not change.

U129.3.p: A washerman who becomes a minister keeps thinking about washing and so fails the king. His old trade ruins his new office.

U130.p: A general idea that long-established habits are hard to break and keep governing behavior even after circumstances change.

U130.1.p: A man who has suddenly become rich still cannot resist the urge to give food to beggars, as he did when he was poor.

U131.p: Getting used to something removes the fear of it. Repeated contact makes a frightening thing seem harmless.

U131.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 60 (ET 224), 111 (ST 224); Halm Aesop No. 39; Jacobs Aesop 208 No. 34.
U131.1.p: A fox who at first feared a lion eventually talks with him freely once the two have become familiar.

U131.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 66 (ET 306), 111 (ST 224); Halm Aesop No. 180.
U131.2.p: People who are at first frightened of a camel eventually take it into their service once they grow used to it.

U133.r: Wienert FFC LVI 81 (ET 474), 111 (ST 226); Halm Aesop No. 368; India: Thompson-Balys.
U133.p: A man soon becomes able to tolerate the foul smells of a tannery, where hides are treated, because he gets used to them.

U133.1.r: Wesselski Mönchslatein 13 No. 8; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
U133.1.p: A farmer prefers the smell of the stable to the smell of flowers. However, the tannery smell, which he got used to, still makes him ill.

U134.p: A knight refuses to go to heaven unless it has hunting dogs, showing how strongly habits and passions persist even after death.

U135.p: Someone or something pines and falls ill when deprived of the food and way of life they are used to.

U135.1.p: At a feast a cat chooses to eat rat meat, which the other animals refuse to touch.

U135.2.p: A shepherd who has been taken into the king's palace becomes sick because he longs for the fresh air of the countryside.

U135.3.p: A man who was once a slave becomes ill from longing for the food he was accustomed to.

U135.3.1.p: A peasant girl who has married a king pines for the simple foods of peasant life.

U135.3.2.p: Peasants who are given white bread ask for the coarse rye bread they are used to.

U136.p: A fisherman and a hunter swap their catches for variety, but soon both go back to the food they started with.

U136.1.p: Discontented workmen swap jobs with one another and become even more unhappy than before.

U136.2.p: Beasts and fishes are made to exchange places, and both die as a result.

U137.p: A mill horse taken to war keeps walking in a circle, because that is what it learned to do at the mill.

U138.p: A person who is dishonest by habit, such as a thief, cannot give up stealing.

U138.1.p: A dishonest silversmith cannot rest until he mixes cheap alloy into the silver ornament he is making.

U138.2.p: Thieves are unable to stop robbing and plundering.

U139.p: Miscellaneous tales showing how strong habit is, not covered by more specific headings.

U139.1.p: A person keeps eating or drinking something out of habit even though it harms them.

U139.2.p: People stick stubbornly to old customs even when it makes no sense to do so.

U139.2.1.p: A people keep a silly and roundabout way of slaughtering a hog out of stubborn tradition.

U140.p: What nourishes one person can poison another.

U141.r: (Cf. U31.) Wienert FFC LVI 84 (ET 512), 121 (ST 303); Halm Aesop No. 25.
U141.p: A fisherman and a man who lives downriver are enemies, because fishing stirs up the water and makes it undrinkable for the other.

U142.r: Wienert FFC LVI 60 (ET 223), 121 (ST 307); Halm Aesop No. 426.
U142.p: An ox enjoys being stroked lovingly by a man, while a flea is frightened by the same caresses.

U143.r: Wienert FFC LVI 85 (ET 513), 121 (ST 305); Halm Aesop No. 59.
U143.p: A collier (charcoal-maker) and a fuller (cloth-cleaner) cannot share a home or living, because the collier blackens whatever he touches while the fuller cleans, so each undoes the other's work.

U144.p: A nightingale refuses to stay with birds whose nest is built of dung, finding their home too filthy for her.

U146.p: A king or other royal person cannot put up with rough, vulgar amusements or coarse entertainment and finds them unbearable.

U146.1.p: A coarse meal or food drives an adulterous king back to his own wife, because he cannot stomach the rough fare of his lover.

U147.p: Animals try to trade their food with one another but none of the exchanges succeed, because each prefers what it already has.

U148.r: Cf. Heywood’s Play of the Weather.
U148.p: Weather that suits one creature or person ruins things for another, so no single kind of weather pleases everyone.

U148.1.p: A bird wants sunshine to dry and warm things while a worm wants clouds and rain so it can come out of the ground.

U149.p: General tale-type heading for the saying that one man's food is another man's poison, with miscellaneous examples of it.

U149.1.p: Lions scorn what donkeys admire, such as braying, which the lions find unpleasant while the donkeys find it beautiful.

U150.p: Heading for stories in which people who are wretched or miserable seem not to care about their troubles or what happens to them.

U151.p: An ass pays no attention when an enemy approaches, reasoning that he could not be any more miserable than he already is.

U160.p: Heading for stories where a person's own fault or carelessness causes the worst of their misfortune.

U161.r: Wienert FFC LVI *64 (ET 277), 117 (ST 273); Halm Aesop No. 4; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
U161.p: An eagle is shot and killed by an arrow that was fletched with one of its own feathers.

U162.r: Wienert FFC LXI *74 (ET 388), 117 (ST 274); Halm Aesop No. 123; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
U162.p: A tree is chopped down with an axe whose handle was made from the tree itself.

U170.p: Heading for stories that show how blind people think, speak, and act, and how others react to them.

U171.p: A blind man crosses a narrow bridge without fear, while his sighted guide is too scared to try it.

U172.p: Two blind men each try to convince the other that he can see, and each manages to fool the other about his blindness.

U173.p: Someone tries in vain to describe the color white to a blind man, and the explanation fails to make sense to him.

U180.p: Heading for the saying that wine reveals the truth, so people tell the truth when drunk.

U181.p: A man cannot get his wife to confess a wrongdoing to the priest, so he gets her drunk and she confesses.

U210.p: A bad ruler produces bad subjects; the people take on the character of their leader.

U211.p: Because there are no great kings any more, there are no great knights either, since the greatness of the ruler shapes the greatness of his followers.

U212.p: A lord can only have loyal, good servants if he himself is good.

U220.p: A peace that is forced on someone by pressure or threat has no real value.

U221.p: A monk, pressed hard by his abbot, forgives a crucifix that has fallen and injured him, but says that the hatred between them will always remain.

U230.p: Stories and sayings about what sin is and how it works on people.

U230.0.1.p: A monk leaves his monastery after seeing a devil there tempting the other brothers. Later, in the world, he sees countless devils tempting ordinary people and returns to the monastery.

U231.p: A hermit rebukes a young man for a sin, then falls into that same sin when he himself is tempted by it.

U231.1.p: A monk scolds his brothers for giving in to temptation, but when he is tested himself he understands how strong temptation is.

U232.r: Alphabet No. 3; Wienert FFC LVI 80 (ET 458), 138 (ST 441); Halm No. 354.
U232.p: No place is secret enough to hide sin from being seen.

U235.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 393; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
U235.p: A father asks about his son and, on hearing the son is a liar, gives him up as hopeless, since lying cannot be cured while other sins can be outgrown.

U235.1.p: A liar cannot be cured even by bathing in the sacred river Ganges.

U236.p: A sick person promises to give up something harmful, such as eating meat, to God in return for recovery, but goes back to the old habit once he is well. For example, a wolf who has overeaten meat vows to eat no more meat, then eats as before when healed.

U236.1.p: A sick rich man repents and gives to the church, but after his death it is found that he planned to take his money back from the church if he recovered.

U240.p: The mind or will can control and affect the physical body, for good or ill.

U241.p: A king wastes away and becomes thin because he is so afraid of dying.

U242.p: Frightened hares, fearing death, are able to outrun the dogs chasing them.

U242.1.r: Succeeds in escaping. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 160*; Prussian: Plenzat 8.
U242.1.p: Surrounded by hunters and hounds, a hare makes his last will, deciding which of his body parts will go to each of his pursuers.

U243.p: With enough courage, one can overcome any obstacle and achieve what seems impossible.

U250.p: Stories and sayings about how short human life is.

U251.r: *Crane Vitry 184 No. 116; Alphabet No. 212; *Mensa Philosophica No. 181.
U251.p: The world is unjust in that young people die as well as old people, so death does not wait for old age. This is the reason a young person may choose to enter a monastery.

U260.p: A general heading for motifs about the passing of time and how it is felt.

U261.p: Time feels short to people who are enjoying themselves and long to people who are waiting. A servant girl gives this answer when her mistress scolds her for coming home late.

U262.p: A person's suffering or grief is eventually cured or eased by the passing of time.

U270.p: People who feel safe and secure become careless and lose their alertness or drive.

U271.p: A cat stops hunting rats once it is given a comfortable home in a monastery. The point is that lazy priests behave the same way once they are comfortable.
